explanations.answer: He goes out to confront Neco
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Neco, king of Egypt, marches up to fight at Carchemish, and "Josiah went out to confront him." Nobody asked Josiah to come out, and he walked right up anyway. I'd have stayed home and checked on my ovens.

explanations.answer: He sends Neco a gift of gold
explanations.explanation: Gold is a nice thought, friend, but the text never mentions a gift. It says Josiah "went out to confront him." Josiah was heading toward Neco, not buying him off. Nobody in this story is passing out envelopes.

explanations.answer: He stays in Jerusalem to pray
explanations.explanation: I like the peaceful picture, baker, but that's not what the text says. It says "Josiah went out to confront him." Josiah left Jerusalem and headed out to meet Neco, king of Egypt. He wasn't the stay-home type that day.

Yes, baker! Neco's messengers say, "I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty." So his message to Josiah was basically, "Not you, friend. Not today." He told Josiah right to his face that this fight wasn't with him.

Close, but the text says otherwise, baker. Neco's messengers tell Josiah, "I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty." So Neco says he has not come against Josiah. His message was "this isn't about you."

That's right, baker. Neco says, "God has told me to hurry." The man was on a deadline, and then a king stepped in front of him. I know that feeling from a cookie order, but my deadlines never come with an army.

Not quite, friend. Neco never says anything about turning back. He says he's fighting another dynasty and that "God has told me to hurry." He's moving forward, and fast. Going home wasn't on his list.
Good guess, since the Euphrates is right there, baker. But Neco says nothing about waiting. He says, "God has told me to hurry." A man told to hurry isn't going to sit down by the water.
Not quite, baker. After the warning, "Josiah, however, did not turn away from him." That "however" tells you which way it went. Josiah heard Neco out and kept going.
That's right, baker. The text says, "Josiah, however, did not turn away from him." Neco gave a clear warning, and Josiah kept going anyway. That "however" is carrying a lot of weight.

You got it, baker. The text says Josiah "did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God." So the warning came from God, spoken through Neco. Josiah missed that, and he went on to fight at the Plain of Megiddo.

Good try, friend, but Egypt's magicians aren't in this passage at all. The text says Josiah "did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God." The words Neco spoke came from God. No magicians needed.
Babylon's king never shows up in this passage, baker. Neco is the one speaking, and the text says his words were "from the mouth of God." That's whose words Josiah didn't listen to.
Not quite, baker. After the archers shoot him, Josiah says, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded!" He doesn't say to keep fighting. He asks to be taken out.
That's right, baker. Josiah says to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded!" There's no "keep fighting" in his words. He was hurt, and he asked to be taken away.

Yes, baker. His servants "brought him to Jerusalem, where he died." They moved him from one chariot to a second chariot and carried him all the way back to the city. I think that was a long, quiet ride.
Megiddo is where the archers shot him, friend, not where he died. The Plain of Megiddo is the battle spot. His servants moved him to his second chariot and "brought him to Jerusalem, where he died."
Carchemish is where Neco was headed, baker, not where Josiah ended up. Josiah never made it that far. His servants "brought him to Jerusalem, where he died."
That's right, baker. The text says, "all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him." The whole land grieved, and I think it was a heavy day for everyone.

His servants were there, since they carried him home, baker. But the text says the mourning was bigger than that: "all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him." The whole land grieved. It wasn't just the people at his side.
Priests and Levites aren't named here, friend. The text says, "all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him." That's the whole land, not one group inside it.
That's it, baker. The singers "established them as a statute for Israel." A statute is a set rule, so these laments weren't a one-time thing. They became a lasting practice in Israel.
A feast makes me happy, friend, but this isn't one. The text says the laments were established "as a statute for Israel." A statute is a set rule, and this one was about mourning.
Good guess, baker, but the word is "statute." The text says they "established them as a statute for Israel." It's a set rule, not a sign. Israel was to keep reciting those laments.

explanations.answer: The Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The rest of Josiah's acts "are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah." His life, from beginning to end, was written down. That's a record I'd want to be in.
The Book of Jashar is a real book, baker, and Joshua 10:13 mentions it. But it's not the one here. Josiah's acts "are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah."

explanations.answer: The Book of the Wars of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That one's real too, friend, and Numbers 21:14 mentions it. But this passage names a different book. Josiah's acts "are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah." Josiah's story isn't over for the Bible, either, so keep your apron on.
